plot_extraction.response_text:
While fishing off Waihee, the skeptical narrator listens irritably as the elderly Hawaiian fisherman Kohokumu chants legends of Maui. When challenged, Kohokumu argues that Maui’s feats are no less reasonable than biblical creation and notes that traditional myths echo truths recognized by modern science.

Their fishing interrupts the debate. Kohokumu, despite being over seventy, dives forty feet, wrestles a huge octopus from a coral crevice, kills it with his teeth, and returns triumphantly. He attributes his vigor to the sea, which he regards as his mother and believes will someday receive and rebirth him. This leads to a philosophical exchange about dreams, truth, identity, and whether reality itself might be Maui’s dream.

To spare the narrator more singing, Kohokumu tells a supposedly factual tale about Keikiwai, an eleven-year-old “Water Baby” who understood the language of fish. When a visiting king demanded lobsters, the people could not gather them because forty sharks infested the lagoon. Keikiwai heard the sharks plotting to eat him and repeatedly announced that the shortest-tailed shark was his protector. Each time he distracted them by throwing a lava rock into the water, dove safely, and returned with a lobster. The suspicious sharks then measured their tails and devoured whichever among them had the shortest. This continued until the final shark, swollen from eating the others, burst and died.

Kohokumu insists the story is true, citing distant family testimony, the actual diving place, and thirty-nine lava rocks he claims still lie on the seabed. Before the narrator can object, hooked fish begin tugging their bamboo poles, and Kohokumu returns to fishing while confidently repeating that he knows the tale for a fact.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts a first-person frame-narrative style in which an educated, sceptical outsider recounts an encounter with an elderly Hawaiian fisherman and oral storyteller. The narrator’s voice is urbane, ironic and self-consciously rational, but his confidence is repeatedly unsettled by Kohokumu’s wit, physical competence and imaginative authority. This creates a productive tension between Western empiricism and indigenous myth: the narrator calls traditional tales “whoppers,” yet notices that modern science oddly echoes some of their claims, while Kohokumu exposes the comparable extravagance of biblical creation. Although the period perspective sometimes carries a patronising, colonial vocabulary, the old fisherman is ultimately the more agile thinker and the dominant personality.

The prevailing tone combines comic irritation, affectionate mockery, adventure and philosophical wonder. Much of the humour comes from reversals: the frail old man is vigorous while the younger narrator is seasick and aching; the supposedly credulous fisherman defeats the rationalist in argument; and solemn myth is punctured by modern jokes, as when the sun is imagined as a trade unionist negotiating a shorter working day. Kohokumu’s shark story develops a broader folktale comedy based on repetition, absurd logic and escalating consequences. Beneath this playfulness lies a reflective, melancholy current concerning age, death, dreams, cultural memory and return to the sea.

The diction moves between several registers. The narrator uses elevated literary language—“Promethean demi-god,” “empery,” “formidable creature”—alongside colloquial judgements such as “bore,” “whopper” and “devilish fine form.” Nautical and naturalistic terms give the setting physical credibility, while Hawaiian words, names and translated expressions root the story in a specific cultural environment. Parenthetical glosses such as “wahine” and “luau” reveal an intended non-Hawaiian readership. Kohokumu’s English is rendered in ceremonious, slightly archaic patterns, including inversions, parallel clauses and vocative forms such as “O Lakana” and “O Young Wise One.” His speech therefore sounds at once translated, biblical and oral-traditional.

Sentence structure is generally expansive and cumulative. Long sentences gather mythic feats, environmental observations or bodily actions through repeated relative clauses and coordinated phrases. These are balanced by short, emphatic exchanges in dialogue, which sharpen the comedy and establish a contest of minds. Repetition is central to the oral texture: formulas recur, sharks perform the same actions in diminishing numbers, and chants employ anaphora and parallelism. Dashes, parentheses, exclamations and ellipses reproduce interruption, qualification and the drifting rhythms of speech. The narrative frequently shifts from descriptive prose into inset song, chant, prayer or tale, giving it a layered, performative quality.

The descriptive style is sensuous and strongly embodied. Heat, glare, stagnant air, nausea and the unstable motion of the outrigger convey the narrator’s discomfort, while the squid episode is rendered with vivid, almost grotesque precision: sliminess, suckers, coiling tentacles and biting teeth make the action tactile and immediate. This realism contrasts with the fantastic content of the legends, yet also supports it. Kohokumu’s extraordinary dive and mastery of the octopus make him seem nearly mythic himself, narrowing the distance between heroic tradition and observable experience. The sea is both a materially exact setting and an archetypal maternal force—dangerous, nourishing and regenerative.

Structurally, the story proceeds by digression rather than by a tightly linear plot. A present-day fishing excursion forms the outer frame, within which chants lead to debate, the squid hunt leads to a meditation on the sea, and a discussion of dreams leads to the embedded Water Baby folktale. The fishing poles repeatedly recall the characters to immediate reality and provide transitions between conversation and action. The embedded tale has the patterned architecture of oral folklore: a crisis is announced, a clever child faces numerous predators, a trick is repeated, and each repetition increases the comic absurdity. Kohokumu closes the story by offering physical “evidence” for an impossible narrative, leaving fact, memory and invention deliberately entangled.

Dialogue is the principal engine of characterization and theme. The narrator questions, interrupts and objects; Kohokumu concedes strategically, counters with analogies, anticipates objections and takes control of the exchange. His answers often turn literal reasoning against scepticism. This produces a Socratic but comic pattern in which categories such as truth, myth, dream and proof become unstable. Kohokumu’s storytelling also dramatizes oral tradition as communal knowledge: truth is guaranteed not by direct observation alone but by inheritance, place, repetition and the persistence of visible signs.

Overall, the style blends travel writing, maritime realism, ethnographic observation, philosophical dialogue and trickster folktale. Its signature qualities are robust sensory description, elaborate oral performance, ironic clashes of worldview, affectionate comic exaggeration and an unresolved movement between the factual and the marvellous. Myth is neither simply endorsed nor dismissed; instead, it becomes a way of expressing truths about nature, ancestry, identity and mortality that rational explanation cannot fully contain.

generation.response_text:
### The Thirty-Nine Stones

We were fishing off Waihee in an outrigger which appeared to have been designed expressly to test the Christian virtues. Its bottom was hard, its gunwale sharp, its shade nonexistent, and its motion compounded the qualities of a cradle, a cork and a drunken horse. The sun stood overhead with the stern attention of an overseer; the wind had gone somewhere else; and the sea, smooth as hammered blue metal, lifted us slowly toward heaven and then, with a private malice, lowered us into the glittering hollow between two swells.

Kohokumu sat in the stern, brown, lean and indestructible. He was more than seventy years old, though he refused arithmetic upon the subject.

“I have lived,” he said, “since before the great wind that took the church roof at Wailuku. Also before the sickness when Pua’s three wives died, one after another, though not so quickly as he wished.”

This information did not help me calculate his age, but it explained something of his philosophy.

He wore a faded cotton shirt, a red loincloth, and an immense wreath of tobacco smoke. His bare feet, twisted by reefs and hardened by lava, grasped the outrigger as naturally as roots grip a cliff. A dozen bamboo poles projected from the canoe. Their lines descended forty feet through a lucid green world where I could see pale sand, antlered coral, and dark fish slipping to and fro like thoughts at the bottom of a dream.

We had been there since dawn. I was burned, cramped, thirsty and intermittently sick. Kohokumu was in devilish fine form. He had eaten two raw sea eggs, half a dried flying fish, and a quantity of poi; he had laughed at my hat; and now, because the fish were not biting, he had begun to sing.

His chant concerned Maui, the Promethean demi-god who hauled islands from the deep, lifted the sky, snared the sun, obtained fire from an ancestress, and performed other public services of a magnitude which would nowadays require several governments, an international loan and a commission of engineers.

Kohokumu sang in a high, quavering voice. Each line seemed to have three beginnings and no end. It mounted, circled, broke upon some sonorous name, and began again. I endured perhaps twenty minutes of it. Then the canoe dipped, my stomach rose, and philosophy deserted me.

“Kohokumu,” I said, “how long is Maui going to continue this performance?”

The old man stopped, his mouth still open upon a vowel.

“O Lakana, he has not yet begun.”

“He has hauled up three islands, beaten the sun, stolen fire, raised the heavens, and tangled the ocean with his fishhook. If that is not a beginning, I tremble to think what the fellow did afterward.”

Kohokumu considered me with mild black eyes.

“Afterward he tried to overcome death.”

“And failed, I hope. Otherwise he must be a great bore by this time.”

“He failed,” said Kohokumu gravely. “Therefore you may be content.”

He resumed the chant.

I seized one of the bamboo poles as if it were a weapon.

“Listen,” I protested. “You are an intelligent man. You know perfectly well that no person fished up an island. Islands are made by volcanic action, coral growth, subsidence, upheaval and a number of other respectable processes.”

“Yes,” he said.

“And no one snared the sun with a rope.”

“No common rope.”

“Nor persuaded it to go slowly for half the year.”

“Why not?”

“Because the sun does not go.”

Kohokumu smiled. “Then Maui was wiser than the song. He caused that which does not go to go more slowly.”

“That is nonsense.”

“Perhaps. Yet you say the days are longer at one season and shorter at another. The old people said Maui bargained with the sun. You say the earth inclines itself and travels around. Both ways, the fishermen gain more daylight in summer. Is the fish concerned with the name of the hook?”

I informed him that an explanation must correspond with observed fact.

He nodded courteously. “And Maui’s bargain corresponds. Before, the sun ran too fast. After, it traveled more gently. The work of men could be finished.”

“The appearance is explained, but the cause is false.”

“Ah,” he said. “You know the cause?”

“Certainly.”

“You have gone outside the sky and watched the earth go around?”

“No.”

“Your father watched?”

“No.”

“His father?”

“Of course not.”

“Then perhaps a man wrote it in a book.”

“A great many men proved it.”

“Men you do not know?”

“Men of science.”

Kohokumu sighed with satisfaction, as though I had confirmed his argument.

“Your ancestors tell you through books. Mine tell me through mouths. Therefore your ancestors speak truth, while mine tell whoppers.”

I had used that word earlier in the morning, and regretted it now.

“There is evidence,” I insisted. “Measurements, calculations, instruments.”

“Our evidence is the length of the day, the time of planting, the season of fish, and the old chant which does not forget.”

“But Maui cannot have been large enough to seize the sun.”

“Your God made the sun.”

“That is different.”

“How?”

Here was the trap, and I stepped into it with the dignity of an educated man.

“The biblical account,” I said, “is not to be taken literally in every particular.”

“Then it is a chant?”

“A spiritual allegory.”

Kohokumu’s face brightened. “Good! Maui also is spiritual allegory.”

“That is not what you were claiming five minutes ago.”

“Five minutes ago you called him a liar. Now you have promoted him.”

I shifted on the hard board, which had by then made an enemy of every bone in my body.

“You cannot compare a primitive legend with the profound symbolism of Genesis.”

“Why not? In your story, light comes before the sun. In Maui’s story, the sun already exists but behaves badly. To me, a badly behaved sun is easier.”

“It depends upon interpretation.”

“All great truths,” Kohokumu said, “depend upon interpretation. That is why priests and lawyers eat well.”

The sea rolled under us. Far inland the mountains of Maui rose through white vapors, their folds deep green and violet. Along the shore, palms shimmered in the glare, and beyond them the cane fields lay in orderly squares, civilized, profitable and quite irrelevant. A tropic bird hung over the water, as still as a white mark painted on the sky.

Kohokumu began another chant.

This one told how, in the first ages, the sky lay so low that men crawled beneath it, unable to stand. Maui braced his shoulders against the blue roof and raised it. The tale, repeated line by line, seemed likely to occupy the afternoon.

“Stop!” I cried. “If Maui lifted the sky, on what did he stand?”

“On the earth.”

“And what supported the earth?”

“The sea.”

“And what supported the sea?”

Kohokumu pointed downward. “Perhaps you should dive and ask.”

At that instant one of the lines twitched. We both became attentive. The bamboo bent, sprang straight, then bent again.

“A fish?” I whispered.

“No. Tako.”

The line jerked toward a patch of coral. Kohokumu hauled it carefully. Something clung below, not hooked, but unwilling to surrender the bait. Twenty feet from the surface a gray shape opened like a foul flower and then contracted. I saw arms uncurl, pale underneath and dark above, with rows of suckers flashing.

The old man looked at it and chuckled.

“Big one.”

“Bring it up.”

“He will release before the canoe.”

“Then hook him.”

“No hook.”

Before I understood his intention, Kohokumu put down the line, stripped off his shirt, and wound a cord around his white hair. The body revealed was narrow and knotted, with ribs like the hoops of a basket, but there was no softness in it. Age had dried him without diminishing him.

“You are not going down there,” I said.

He slipped a short wooden knife into his loincloth.

“Forty feet,” I continued. “And that creature is the size of a washtub.”

“Tako is good eating.”

“It may eat you first.”

“He has no poi.”

Then Kohokumu filled his lungs and went over the side.

He entered without a splash. The surface closed, and through it I watched him descend, brown back diminishing in the green. He did not swim as I swam, with much labor and little result. He folded himself and fell headfirst, giving an occasional movement of his feet. The octopus had let go of the bait and flowed into a coral crevice.

At the bottom Kohokumu settled on his knees.

For a moment he was hidden by a burst of sand. Then an arm whipped out and wound around his wrist. Another caught his shoulder. The old man thrust both hands into the hole. More arms emerged—gray, muscular and horribly intimate. They crawled over his chest, looped his neck and clung to his face. The water darkened with ink.

I gripped the outrigger. My heart performed all the activity which Kohokumu’s heart, at that depth, wisely avoided. Twenty seconds passed. Thirty. Forty.

The black cloud thinned. Inside it there was a confusion of legs, arms and tentacles. Kohokumu’s heels braced against the reef. He pulled. The octopus spread itself across the coral, suckers clinging with such force that I could see the flesh draw taut between them. Kohokumu twisted, released one arm, tore another loose, and suddenly came backward with the whole formidable creature upon him.

He kicked toward the surface.

The octopus covered his head. Its mantle bulged above his brow like a monstrous cap; two arms streamed behind; the others tightened around his throat and body. Halfway up he seized the mantle, dragged it to his mouth, and bit between the eyes.

I saw the bite distinctly.

He bit again.

The arms loosened. Kohokumu rose beside the canoe and exploded into air, spitting seawater and laughter. I hauled at his shoulder while he pushed the octopus before him. Together we dropped it into the bottom.

Even dead, it seemed reluctant to accept the change in circumstances. Its arms writhed over our feet, the suckers fastening and releasing with obscene little kisses. One coiled around my ankle. I shouted and kicked, nearly capsizing us. Kohokumu fell against the gunwale, laughing until tears ran down his cheeks.

“O Young Wise One! Behold! He desires your scientific explanation!”

I freed myself with the fish knife and retired as far as one may retire in a twelve-foot canoe.

Kohokumu sat down, breathing easily. A thin line of blood ran from his cheek where a sucker had torn the skin. He wiped it with his shirt, recovered the bait, and reset the line.

“You are over seventy,” I said.

“Perhaps.”

“You stayed below nearly a minute.”

“Perhaps.”

“That animal might have drowned you.”

“Not today.”

“And you killed it with your teeth.”

“My teeth are old, but the tako did not know.”

He patted the dead creature affectionately.

“What keeps you alive?” I asked. “You smoke, you have never consulted a doctor, you eat things which civilized digestion refuses even to name, and you perform feats that would rupture a man of thirty.”

“The sea keeps me.”

“The sea kills men.”

“So does bread, when there is none.”

He leaned over, scooped water in his hands, and poured it over his face. In that gesture there was no theatrical reverence. It was intimate and careless, like a child rubbing his cheek against his mother’s skirt.

“She made us,” he said. “Before men walked, they swam. Before the bird flew, its grandfather moved in water. Before your thoughts learned to speak, they floated in darkness.”

I stared at him.

“That,” I admitted, “is surprisingly close to certain scientific theories.”

Kohokumu showed his worn teeth. “Then your scientists are learning the old chant.”

“You cannot possibly know the doctrine of evolution.”

“I know that the crab does not grow on the mountain. I know the child rests in water inside the wahine—woman—before he sees the sun. I know the turtle comes from the sea, lays its eggs on land, and returns. A man needs no spectacles to see that life travels.”

“That is observation, not proof.”

“Proof is an observation wearing shoes.”

He pointed toward the blue depths.

“My mother is below. Not the woman who bore me; she was Kalua, and she had a loud voice and a heavy hand. The older mother is below. Someday I shall go into her. She will close over me. The little fish will take my flesh, the coral my bones, and perhaps I shall come again.”

“As what?”

“A shark, if I remain greedy. A turtle, if I become wise. A small silver fish, if I learn obedience.”

“And if you learn none of these?”

“Then I shall return as a storyteller and trouble another Lakana.”

The sun had moved westward, though by Kohokumu’s account this was doubtless the result of an ancient labor dispute between Maui and the solar body. A faint breeze roughened the sea. The ridges inland became dark, and one long cloud unfolded above them like smoke from a sacrificial fire.

“Do you literally believe you will be born again?” I asked.

“Do you literally believe you are awake?”

I laughed. “At present my bruises are convincing.”

“In a dream, pain is also convincing.”

“But I awaken.”

“Perhaps death is awakening.”

“That is merely a metaphor.”

“Perhaps this is merely a metaphor.”

He waved one hand, including the canoe, the mountains, the dead octopus and my aching person.

I told him that if reality were a dream, it was a singularly uncomfortable one.

“Whose dream?” he asked.

“Yours, apparently.”

“No. In my dream you are not so argumentative.”

“Then mine.”

“In your dream I would be younger, so that my strength should not shame you.”

There was no safe route through this discussion.

Kohokumu drew up one line, inspected the untouched hook, and dropped it again. “Perhaps we are dreamed by Maui. Perhaps Maui sits beyond the horizon, sleeping after his labors. He dreams islands, suns, fish, old men and strangers with books inside their heads. When he turns in sleep, the earth shakes. When he sighs, the trade wind blows. When he awakens—puff!—where then is Lakana?”

“Where, for that matter, is Kohokumu?”

The old man shrugged. “I am in the story. That is enough.”

“You confuse truth with imagination.”

“No. You separate them too sharply. A net with holes too small catches water and loses fish.”

“I prefer facts.”

“Then I shall tell you a fact.”

“Not another song.”

“No song.”

“Nor a legend.”

“No legend.”

“Nor anything concerning Maui.”

“Maui will not enter.”

“Nor a man who turns into a shark, a pig who marries a princess, a stone that gives birth, a lizard longer than Lahaina, or an ancestor who climbs a rainbow.”

“None of these.”

I settled myself suspiciously. “Proceed.”

“This happened at Honokohau when my mother’s grandfather’s elder sister was young.”

“That is not a promising beginning.”

“It happened at the place where the black cliff makes a half-moon and the freshwater comes through the stones beneath the sea. The hole is there. The stones are there. The family is known. Therefore it is fact.”

“I reserve judgment.”

“You reserve it as a miser reserves money. Listen.

“In that time there lived a boy called Keikiwai—the Water Baby. Eleven years old he was: small in the shoulders, quick in the hands, with hair burned red by sun and skin that shone when wet. He slept beside the surf. He could remain underwater longer than a priest can remain at a feast, and he understood the speech of fish.

“You do not believe fish speak.”

“I promised only to listen.”

“Good. Then your disbelief may sit behind you and be quiet.

“Keikiwai knew the warning cry of the small reef fish when the ulua hunted. He knew the gossip of parrotfish, who complain while eating and eat while complaining. He knew the lobster’s prayer when the moon is dark. He knew the speech of sharks, which is simple and concerns chiefly hunger.

“At this time a king visited Honokohau. He arrived with paddlers, warriors, priests, drummers, three fat counselors and a wife whose appetite was more powerful than any of them. The people made a luau—a feast—with pig, poi, mullet, seaweed, bananas, breadfruit and sweet potatoes. But the king’s wife looked upon these things and said, ‘Where are the lobsters?’

“The headman trembled, because when a king’s wife asks where something is, a wise man does not answer that it is somewhere else.

“Now, in the lagoon were many lobsters, red and thick and excellent. But forty sharks had entered through the reef passage. Forty! They lay in the green water from the freshwater spring to the black cliff, and for three days no man had dared dive.

“The headman called the fishermen.

“‘Bring lobsters.’

“The fishermen looked at the sharks.

“‘Our eyes are weak,’ they said. ‘We see no lobsters.’

“The headman called the young men.

“‘Bring lobsters.’

“The young men rubbed their stomachs and said they had eaten something harmful.

“Then Keikiwai stepped forward.

“‘I shall bring them.’

“His mother struck him on the head. His aunt struck his mother for raising a foolish son. His grandmother struck them both and said the boy had spoken before the king and must now either dive or be killed for mockery. Thus the family settled the matter.

“Keikiwai took a basket and walked to the cliff. The forty sharks saw him.

“‘Here comes food,’ said the shark with the longest tail.

“‘Small food,’ said the next.

“‘Tender food,’ said the third.

“‘Mine,’ said all forty.

“Keikiwai heard them. At the edge of the lagoon he bent and picked up a piece of black lava. Then he called:

“‘Eat me if you wish, O sharks! Yet I warn you: the shark with the shortest tail is my protector.’

“At this the sharks became uneasy.

“‘Which has the shortest tail?’ asked the first.

“‘Not I,’ said the second.

“‘Certainly not I,’ said the third.

“Every shark turned to inspect his neighbor’s tail, but a shark cannot measure well while swimming, and no shark considers his own tail short.

“Keikiwai threw the lava stone far to the right.

“Splash!

“All forty sharks rushed toward the sound. Keikiwai dived to the left, went down to the ledge, placed one large lobster in his basket, and returned to shore.

“The king’s wife ate it.

“‘Another,’ she said.

“The next day Keikiwai came again. The sharks had spent the night discussing him.

“‘He escaped,’ said the longest-tailed shark.

“‘Because his protector warned him,’ said another.

“‘Who is the protector?’

“‘The one with the shortest tail.’

“They tried to compare their tails. They swam side by side. They swam in circles. They lined themselves against the cliff, but the tide moved them. At last one cried:

“‘There! That fellow’s tail is shorter than mine!’

“The others looked. Since they were hungry and tired of measuring, they agreed.

“They ate him.

“Thus there remained thirty-nine sharks.

“Keikiwai came to the edge with his basket.

“‘Eat me if you wish, O sharks! Yet the shark with the shortest tail is my protector.’

“The thirty-nine sharks looked at one another.

“Keikiwai threw a stone.

“Splash!

“They rushed to the right; he dived to the left; he took a lobster and returned.

“The king’s wife ate it.

“‘Another,’ she said.”

Kohokumu paused to examine his lines.

“You intend to repeat this thirty-nine times,” I said.

“The thing happened thirty-nine times.”

“The tale will not.”

“O Lakana, truth cannot be hurried.”

“Summarize.”

He looked injured, but complied.

“Each night the sharks measured tails. Each night they found the shortest. Each night they ate him. Each morning Keikiwai cried, ‘The shortest-tailed shark is my protector!’ Each morning he threw a stone—splash!—and while they hunted the sound, he dived for a lobster.

“After the fifth day, there were thirty-five sharks.

“After the tenth, thirty.

“After the twentieth, twenty.

“They became fat. They became suspicious. They also became poor at counting, for the shark who had counted heads was eaten on the seventh night, and the shark who replaced him could count only as high as the number of fins he could see without turning.

“When twelve remained, they held a council.

“‘This boy deceives us,’ said one.

“‘Impossible,’ said another. ‘He tells us plainly that the shortest-tailed shark protects him.’

“‘Then why does the protector allow us to eat him?’

“‘Because we always eat the wrong shark.’

“This seemed reasonable.

“They measured again.

“The next morning there were eleven.

“Keikiwai came.

“‘Eat me if you wish—’

“‘We know!’ cried the sharks. ‘The shortest tail!’

“He threw the stone.

“Splash!

“They rushed to the right. He dived left, and the king’s wife received her twenty-ninth lobster.

“When only four sharks remained, each was enormous, having eaten so many of his companions. Their bellies dragged near the sand, and they could no longer turn quickly. Nevertheless, hunger is a hole that grows wider when filled.

“The four placed their tails together.

“‘Yours is shortest,’ said the first to the second.

“‘No, yours,’ said the second to the third.

“‘The fourth has hidden part of his tail under a rock,’ said the third.

“The fourth denied it.

“They quarreled until moonrise and then ate the first, because he had begun the argument.

“Three remained.

“On the following day Keikiwai threw his thirty-eighth stone—”

“Thirty-eighth?” I interrupted. “By my count it should not be.”

“Your count is foreign. Mine is family count.”

“Arithmetic has no nationality.”

“Then why do merchants and fishermen never agree?”

He went on.

“The three rushed to the splash. Keikiwai brought up a lobster.

“That night the three sharks agreed there could be no safety while any tail remained unmeasured. They bit one another’s tails to make them equal. But the first bit too much from the second, and the third laughed. So the second and third ate the first.

“Two remained, each so swollen that he resembled a canoe house with fins.

“‘Your tail is shorter,’ said one.

“‘Your eyes are crooked,’ said the other.

“They placed their noses against the cliff and stretched their tails toward the sea. A wave moved the first forward. The second declared this cheating. They fought, and the stronger ate the weaker, though with difficulty, because there was very little room remaining inside him.

“Now there was one shark.

“He was the longest shark, the shortest shark, the fattest shark and the thinnest shark in the lagoon. He was also, by necessity, Keikiwai’s protector.

“On the next morning the boy came with his basket. The final shark waited beneath the cliff.

“Keikiwai called, ‘Eat me if you wish, O shark! Yet the shark with the shortest tail is my protector.’

“The shark looked behind him. There was no other tail.

“‘I am the protector,’ he said.

“‘So you are,’ said Keikiwai.

“‘Then you have lied. I shall eat you.’

“‘Before you eat me, measure your tail.’

“‘Against what?’

“‘Against the place where the tails of the other sharks ended.’

“The shark swam to the rocks where the measuring had occurred. Because he was swollen with thirty-nine sharks—”

“Thirty-nine?” I said. “If there were forty originally, and he is the last, he could have eaten, directly or indirectly—”

“O Divider of Fish Bones, be silent. He was swollen with thirty-nine sharks. Keikiwai lifted the thirty-ninth lava stone.

“‘Your tail is indeed the shortest,’ the boy said.

“The shark twisted to see. But his belly was too great. He twisted harder. Inside him were sharks which had eaten sharks which had eaten sharks. Their fins and teeth pressed one upon another like angry people in a small house.

“Keikiwai threw the stone.

“Splash!

“The shark lunged toward it from long habit.

“His belly struck a pinnacle of coral.

“Pop!”

Kohokumu clapped his hands so sharply that I started.

“He burst. Out came tails, fins, teeth, bones, greed, argument and bad arithmetic. The water boiled. Crabs hid. The king’s counselors fled uphill. Keikiwai dived quietly, selected the finest lobster in the lagoon, and carried it to the king’s wife.

“She looked at it and said, ‘I am tired of lobster. Have you no chicken?’

“Therefore,” Kohokumu concluded, “the people of Honokohau remember Keikiwai, who saved the divers by feeding sharks to themselves.”

For a little while there was only the wash of water against the hull and the faint ticking of suckers as the dead octopus relaxed at our feet.

“That,” I said at last, “is the factual account you promised?”

“Yes.”

“A boy understood sharks.”

“Yes.”

“Forty sharks successively ate one another because he announced that the shortest-tailed one protected him.”

“Exactly.”

“The last consumed thirty-nine and burst upon coral.”

“You listened well.”

“And there are thirty-nine stones?”

“Below the cliff.”

“Why not forty?”

“The first day he did not need a stone.”

“You said he picked one up.”

“He picked it up, but perhaps he did not throw it.”

“You said he threw it.”

“Then one stone was carried away by the current.”

“You have an answer for everything.”

“No. Only for questions.”

I demanded his evidence.

Kohokumu raised one finger. “My mother’s grandfather’s elder sister heard the tale from Keikiwai’s daughter.”

“Not from Keikiwai?”

“He was dead.”

“Convenient.”

“Death often is.”

A second finger rose. “The diving hole remains. You may see it.”

“A lagoon proves no talking fish.”

A third finger. “The black cliff is there.”

“Cliffs are notoriously careless about corroboration.”

A fourth. “The freshwater rises beneath the salt water, as the tale says.”

“That could be observed by anyone.”

A fifth. “The thirty-nine stones lie below.”

“Lava stones lie everywhere in these islands.”

“Not those stones.”

“What distinguishes them?”

“They are the stones Keikiwai threw.”

I looked at him helplessly.

He smiled, benevolent in victory. “Also, when I was a boy, an old woman of Honokohau had a lobster shell. It came from the last lobster.”

“You saw this shell?”

“I saw a shell.”

“How did you know it was the shell?”

“She told me.”

“And how did she know?”

“Her grandmother told her.”

Thus did the fortress of evidence close its gates.

“You call that knowledge?”

“Yes.”

“It is hearsay, tradition, coincidence and invention.”

“It is family, place, memory and stones.”

“The stones prove nothing.”

“Then dive and count them.”

“And if there are thirty-nine?”

“You will say someone placed them there.”

“Naturally.”

“And if there are thirty-eight, you will say I lied.”

“Naturally.”

“And if there are forty?”

“I shall say you counted badly.”

Kohokumu laughed. “Behold the open mind of the man of science! It is a door with three locks.”

Before I could frame a reply, the bamboo poles sprang alive.

One bent almost double. Another rattled across the gunwale. A third jerked from its notch and would have vanished had Kohokumu not caught it with his toes. Instantly the philosopher disappeared and the fisherman took his place.

“Pull, Lakana! Pull!”

I seized the nearest pole. The line cut sideways, humming. Far below, silver bodies flashed over the coral. Kohokumu hauled hand over hand, shouting instructions, abuse and encouragement in two languages. A fish broke the surface beside the canoe, scarlet as fire, thrashing spray into our faces. My own line came up with two shining akule twisting upon it. The outrigger rocked; the dead octopus slid against my feet; hooks glittered; fish beat the boards like sudden rain.

For ten minutes there was no room in the world for mythology. There were only lines to clear, hooks to free, bait to save and the splendid, practical fact of fish.

At last the school passed. The poles straightened. Sixteen fish lay in the bottom, bright scales dimming beside the monstrous tako. Kohokumu rebaited his hooks with swift brown fingers. His breath remained untroubled.

I looked toward the shore, where evening had begun to gather purple in the valleys. Somewhere beyond those ridges lay Honokohau, its black cliff, its spring beneath the sea, and, conceivably, thirty-nine ordinary stones upon which an extraordinary certainty had been built.

“Kohokumu,” I began.

He held up a warning hand.

“No more questions. The fish are returning.”

“But about Keikiwai—”

“I know it for a fact.”

“You cannot know—”

“For a fact, O Lakana.”

The tip of his pole dipped. He leaned forward, smiling at the water.

“For a fact,” he repeated, and struck.

## The Lighthouse That Remembered

On the morning the lighthouse began to speak, Mara Venn was repairing a clock that had not worked in forty-three years.

The clock belonged to Mrs. Bell, who had inherited it from an uncle no one in the village remembered. Its wooden case was swollen with damp, its hands were fixed at seventeen minutes past six, and a small brass moon stared from the dial with an expression of permanent surprise.

“It stopped the night my husband proposed,” Mrs. Bell had told Mara. “I thought it might be pleasant to hear it tick again.”

Mara did not believe that broken things cared about sentiment. Springs weakened, salt corroded metal, and people attached stories to the damage. Still, she had accepted the clock and placed it on the workbench by her window.

Outside, the village of Valehook leaned against the coast as if resisting the sea. Its cottages were built of gray stone. Fishing boats rocked in the harbor. Above them all, on a black cliff beyond the eastern road, stood the lighthouse.

No keeper had lived there for twenty years. The lamp was automatic now, maintained twice a year by engineers from the mainland. Every evening it sent a white blade across the water, steady and indifferent.

At ten minutes past nine, as Mara was lifting the clock’s balance wheel with a pair of tweezers, a voice rolled over the village.

“Elsinore,” it said.

The windows trembled.

Mara’s tweezers slipped. The balance wheel bounced once and vanished beneath the workbench.

For several seconds there was silence. Then doors opened along the street.

“What was that?” shouted someone.

The voice came again, deep and hollow, carried from the direction of the lighthouse.

“Elsinore. Red sails. Three bells before dawn.”

A flock of gulls rose from the rooftops. In the harbor, dogs began barking.

Mara stepped outside. Her neighbor, Tomas Rill, stood in the road wearing one boot and holding the other.

“Did the lighthouse just say ‘Elsinore’?” he asked.

“It sounded like it.”

“What’s Elsinore?”

“I don’t know.”

By noon, everyone had an answer.

Elsinore was a ship, a woman, a vanished kingdom, or a kind of fever. Old Captain Stroud insisted that he had once drunk with a Dane named Elsinore in a port south of nowhere. The schoolmaster produced an atlas and found three towns with similar names, none nearby. Mrs. Bell said it might be a warning from the dead.

The mayor sent two constables to the lighthouse. They returned before sunset, pale and offended.

“The door’s locked,” said Constable Hake.

“You have keys,” Mara reminded him.

“The keys don’t fit anymore.”

That night, half the village gathered on the sea wall.

Clouds covered the moon. The lighthouse beam crossed the black water, passed over the village, and vanished among the hills. Each time it swept above them, the crowd grew still.

At midnight, the voice spoke again.

“Elsinore entered the northern channel under red sails. Her captain mistook the bells. Two hundred and six souls. The sea received them.”

The final words faded into the wind.

No one laughed.

The next morning, wreckage washed ashore.

There were planks blackened by age, a cracked mast, a child’s wooden shoe, and a ship’s bell green with corrosion. Across the bell, beneath weeds and barnacles, someone found a name.

ELSINORE.

The schoolmaster searched the village archives. Mara went with him, less from curiosity than from the conviction that every mystery had a mechanism.

They found the account in a leather book dated 1711.

The Elsinore had carried families fleeing a distant war. During a storm, the crew had mistaken Valehook’s chapel bells for a harbor signal. The ship turned north instead of south and struck the reef below the lighthouse cliff. There were no survivors.

“But there was no lighthouse in 1711,” Mara said.

“No,” replied the schoolmaster. “It was built because of the wreck.”

Mara looked toward the tower through the archive window.

“Then how does it know?”

The schoolmaster closed the book. “That is a question for someone who repairs old things.”

“I repair clocks.”

“Time seems relevant.”

For three days, the lighthouse remained silent.

People climbed the cliff and laid flowers at its locked door. The child’s shoe was placed in the chapel. The ship’s bell was hung near the harbor, where the wind sometimes moved its clapper and produced a note too soft to be heard from shore.

Then, on Thursday afternoon, the lighthouse spoke a second name.

“Merrowfield.”

This time the village listened.

“High tide. Western wind. The hillside opened at half past two.”

Merrowfield was the farm above Valehook. Its owner, Ena Marr, had lived there alone since her sons left for the city. The mayor ordered the constables to investigate. They found nothing except sheep, wet grass, and Ena angrily baking bread.

At two fifteen the next morning, rain began to fall.

Mara woke from a dream of ticking clocks. She lay in darkness, listening to water strike the roof. Then she remembered the lighthouse’s words.

Half past two.

She dressed, took her coat and lantern, and ran uphill.

Others had remembered too. Tomas Rill was ahead of her, carrying a shovel. Constable Hake followed with a rope. They reached Merrowfield as Ena opened the door and demanded to know why half the village was trampling her cabbages.

At two twenty-nine, the hillside groaned.

The sound was low and vast, like stone waking beneath the earth.

“Run!” Mara shouted.

They dragged Ena from the doorway. A moment later, the rain-soaked slope gave way. Mud, rock, and uprooted trees crashed through the farmhouse, crushing the kitchen where the oven still burned.

No one died.

After that, the lighthouse’s words became law.

It spoke every few days, sometimes of the past and sometimes of what had not yet happened.

“Dove Street,” it announced, “where the blue door burns.”

The family behind the blue door was moved. That night, a chimney fire destroyed their house.

“Little Sam Vey. Below the western pier. The tide is coming in.”

Fishermen found Sam unconscious beneath the pier after he had fallen from the sea wall.

“Three boats. Fog. Do not follow the silver light.”

The fishing fleet stayed in harbor. Through the fog, villagers saw a pale glow drifting above the reef, though no vessel was there.

Valehook changed.

People stopped making decisions without glancing toward the lighthouse. Weddings were delayed in case it objected. Children dared one another to shout their names at the tower and ask how they would die. Merchants postponed journeys. Fishermen refused to sail on days when the lamp looked unusually bright.

Mara watched with growing unease.

The lighthouse had saved lives. She could not deny it. Yet clocks had taught her that knowing the hour did not grant power over time. Often it only made one anxious about being late.

One winter evening, Tomas came into her shop carrying a pocket watch.

“Can you stop it?” he asked.

“That’s generally the opposite of my work.”

He placed the watch on the bench. It was silver and finely made. Mara heard its rapid, healthy ticking.

“It belonged to my father,” Tomas said. “The lighthouse spoke his name last night.”

Mara looked up. She had slept through the announcement.

“What did it say?”

“‘Arlen Rill. The winter crossing. Beneath the ice.’”

“Your father died thirty years ago.”

“He disappeared thirty years ago. His boat was found empty.”

Tomas sat by the window. Outside, snow drifted between the cottages.

“My mother always said he ran away,” he continued. “She waited for him until she died. If she’d known…”

He did not finish.

Mara opened the back of the watch. Inside, engraved on the case, were the words: For Arlen—Come Home Before Dark.

“The lighthouse tells us what happened,” Tomas said. “But it tells us too late.”

“Not always.”

“No. Sometimes it tells us just in time. Which is worse, perhaps.”

Mara studied him.

“Why?”

“Because now we think every silence is permission.”

That night, Mara climbed to the lighthouse alone.

The path was hard with frost. The sea below was invisible, but she heard waves striking the cliff. The lighthouse beam passed above her in white intervals, illuminating grass, stone, and the iron door.

She examined the lock.

The constables had been correct: the village key did not fit. But locks were only mechanisms, and mechanisms could be persuaded.

After twenty minutes with wire, oil, and language Mrs. Bell would not have approved of, Mara felt the final pin rise.

The door opened inward.

A spiral stair climbed through darkness. The walls smelled of salt and cold iron. Mara raised her lantern and began to ascend.

On the first landing, she found names scratched into the stone.

Some she recognized: Elsinore. Merrowfield. Sam Vey.

Most she did not.

Thousands of names covered the walls, written in charcoal, ink, pencil, paint, and rust. Some had dates beside them. Others were accompanied by short phrases.

At sea.

Under the hill.

The red sickness.

Home before dark.

Mara climbed faster.

The second landing held pieces of the past: a broken compass, a woman’s ring, a fisherman’s knife, letters tied with blue ribbon, a toy horse, buttons, bones. They had been arranged carefully in circles around the stairs.

At the top, beneath the turning lamp, she found the machinery.

There were no loudspeakers, no wires from the mainland, no hidden rooms. Only gears.

Hundreds of them filled the lantern chamber, rising from floor to ceiling. Brass teeth turned against iron. Chains passed through pulleys. Pendulums swung in different rhythms, some slowly, some so quickly they trembled. At the center stood a clock with no hands.

Mara approached it.

The clock face bore only one word:

LISTEN.

She placed her palm against the case.

The machinery stopped.

In the sudden quiet, the sea seemed to inhale.

Then the lighthouse spoke, not across the village but inside the room.

“Mara Venn.”

She drew back.

“The last light. The broken stair. Dawn does not come.”

Mara waited for more, but the gears began moving again.

She fled.

For the next week, she told no one.

She considered dismantling the mechanism, but the warning had mentioned a broken stair. If she returned and the stair broke, would she cause the prediction by trying to prevent it? If she stayed away, would someone else climb and fall?

And what did “the last light” mean? What did it mean that dawn did not come?

Her work suffered. Mrs. Bell’s clock gained nine minutes an hour. A sailor’s watch began running backward after Mara replaced its spring. At night she dreamed of the lighthouse calling every name in Valehook, one after another, until the sea rose and covered the village.

Then the tower fell silent.

A day passed, then two.

On the third night, its lamp went out.

Panic spread before sunrise. Boats returned to harbor. The mayor sent a telegram to the mainland. Engineers could not arrive for two days because a storm was moving along the coast.

“We need to light it ourselves,” said Constable Hake.

Mara stared toward the dark cliff.

“The stair is unsafe,” she said.

“You’ve been inside?”

She admitted that she had.

By evening, the storm had arrived. Wind tore tiles from roofs. Waves broke over the harbor wall. Far out at sea, a ship sounded its horn.

The vessel was approaching Valehook without a guiding light.

“We have to go,” Tomas said.

Mara remembered the words: The last light. The broken stair. Dawn does not come.

“If I enter that tower, I die.”

Tomas did not ask how she knew.

He looked toward the sea, where the ship’s horn sounded again.

“Perhaps,” he said. “Or perhaps it only wants you to believe you do.”

They climbed together.

Inside the lighthouse, the names on the walls gleamed with moisture. The tower shook in the wind. Tomas carried fuel; Mara carried tools.

Halfway up, an iron step snapped beneath her foot.

She fell.

Tomas caught her wrist. For an instant, she hung above the dark spiral, her boots striking stone. Then he pulled her onto the landing.

“The broken stair,” she whispered.

“But not the end,” he said.

They continued upward.

The machinery in the lantern room was still. The lamp’s great lens faced the sea like a blind eye. Mara inspected the fuel line and ignition system. Both were intact.

“It should work,” she said.

“Then why doesn’t it?”

The handless clock stood open.

Inside was an empty space shaped like a heart. A small brass fitting waited at its center, but whatever had once been attached there was gone.

Mara thought of the ship’s bell, the child’s shoe, the rings and letters arranged below. Objects carried memory because people gave it to them. Clocks ticked because springs held tension. Lighthouses spoke because—

Because something had been winding them.

She took Mrs. Bell’s clock from her bag.

She had carried it without knowing why. Perhaps because it was unfinished, or because its frozen hands had measured the moment before one life became another.

“What are you doing?” Tomas asked.

“Repairing an old thing.”

She removed the clock’s mainspring. It was delicate, spotted with rust, and too small for the brass fitting. She bent the outer coil, tightened it with pliers, and fixed it into the empty heart of the lighthouse clock.

For a moment, nothing happened.

Then the spring turned.

One gear moved, followed by another.

Pendulums swung. Chains rose. The lens shuddered and began to rotate.

Light burst across the chamber.

Outside, the ship’s horn answered.

But the machinery accelerated. Gears screamed. The floor trembled.

Names began pouring from the lighthouse, spoken in overlapping voices.

“Lysa Trent—”

“Harbor Road—”

“The autumn fever—”

“Beneath the white tree—”

“Jon Vale—”

“Tomorrow, tomorrow, tomorrow—”

Mara covered her ears.

The tower was not merely remembering. It was choking on memory, crowded with every loss that had ever touched the coast and every loss that might yet come.

The spring glowed red.

“It can’t hold!” Tomas shouted.

Mara reached for it, but the heat drove her back.

The lighthouse spoke her name again.

“Mara Venn. The last light. The broken stair. Dawn does not come.”

The walls cracked.

She understood then.

The warning was not a verdict. It was a memory the tower had not yet learned how to place. Dawn did not come because the mechanism could see only darkness. It knew disasters, endings, and grief. No one had taught it to remember what happened afterward.

Mara seized a metal bar and drove it between the gears.

The machinery shrieked.

“What are you doing?” Tomas cried.

“Teaching it to stop.”

She pushed harder. Gear teeth shattered. Chains snapped and whipped through the chamber. The clock face split from top to bottom.

For one terrible second, the lamp went dark.

Then the fuel caught.

A steady flame rose inside the lens.

The lighthouse beam crossed the sea.

Below, the hidden ship altered course.

Mara and Tomas descended as the first edge of morning appeared beyond the storm. The broken stair remained broken, but they stepped over it.

By sunrise, the wind had weakened. Villagers gathered on the cliff, cheering when Mara emerged.

The lighthouse never spoke again.

Some people mourned its silence. Others were relieved. The mayor ordered the door repaired, though Mara kept the old key. Engineers replaced the shattered gears with an ordinary lamp mechanism, simple and reliable.

Months later, Mrs. Bell returned to the workshop.

“Is my clock finished?” she asked.

Mara placed it on the counter.

The hands were still fixed at seventeen minutes past six.

“I’m sorry,” Mara said. “I couldn’t make it run.”

Mrs. Bell listened to the silence inside the wooden case.

“That’s all right,” she said at last. “My husband was late that evening anyway. He proposed at half past seven.”

She laughed and carried the clock home.

Years passed. Valehook continued as villages do, by weathering what came. Children grew. Boats departed and returned. Fires were extinguished, storms survived, and some warnings arrived too late.

Mara became known as the finest clock repairer on the coast, though she never claimed she could fix everything.

When people asked about the night the lighthouse spoke her name, she gave different answers. Sometimes she said it had predicted her death and been wrong. Sometimes she said it had predicted its own.

But on quiet evenings, when the beam crossed her workshop window, she would pause and listen.

Not for voices.

For the ordinary sounds beneath them: the ticking of repaired clocks, the harbor bell, footsteps in the street, laughter from the inn, and waves withdrawing over stones.

Things ending.

Things beginning.

Time, moving because no one had asked it to remember everything.
